title: Ultrasonic Testing for Offshore Platforms | UT (US Gulf)
description: On-site ultrasonic testing for Gulf of Mexico platforms and yards: thickness surveys, risers, topsides piping and weld UT to AWS D1.1. Request a UT quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Testing for Offshore Platforms and Fabrication Yards in the United States
html:
Atlantis NDT provides ultrasonic testing (UT) for offshore oil and gas assets in the United States: thickness surveys on topsides piping, vessels, risers and splash zone members, and weld examination on platform structure and fabricated modules. Work happens on Gulf of Mexico platforms, at onshore fabrication yards and at supply bases, with technicians mobilized for the agreed scope. To scope a job, request a UT inspection quote with your structure or piping data.

What UT covers on an offshore platform

A fixed platform in the Gulf is a structure, a process plant and a lifting system sharing one deck. UT serves all three. On the structure, thickness gauging tracks wall loss in jacket legs and braces, risers, conductors, caissons and boat-landing members, where seawater and wave action eat steel from the outside. On the process side, it measures piping, separators and scrubbers on the topsides, along with firewater and utility systems. On the lifting side, it checks the weld areas of crane pedestals and boom sections where the crane maker and API guidance call for volumetric examination.

The common thread is that offshore corrosion is localized and driven by the environment: salt spray, wet-dry cycling, trapped moisture under insulation and coatings, and microbial attack inside produced-water lines. A thickness grid that follows the damage pattern finds it. A single spot reading does not.

Regulators and codes that shape the work

In federal waters of the Gulf of Mexico, the Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement regulates oil and gas operations under 30 CFR Part 250, including requirements for platform structures and for the operator's safety and environmental management system. The operator's inspection program turns those rules into scopes, usually through API RP 2A for fixed platforms and the structural integrity management practice published by API. Fabricated structural steel follows AWS D1.1, topsides piping follows ASME B31.3, and offshore cranes follow API Spec 2C for new units and API RP 2D for operation and inspection.

Atlantis supplies examination data under these programs. We do not set inspection intervals, calculate remaining life, or decide fitness for service; the operator's engineer or integrity group uses our readings for that. Underwater inspection by divers or remote vehicles is a separate specialty that we do not offer.

Thickness surveys in the splash zone and above

The splash zone, the band of a leg or riser that is alternately wetted and dried by waves, is the most corrosion-prone part of a jacket. Above water, thickness testing is practical on exposed members once marine growth and coating are removed. Surveys follow a defined grid around the circumference at set elevations, with readings logged against a clock position so repeat surveys line up. Splash zone wraps and sleeves, where installed, hide the steel; the survey is taken at the wrap edges and, where the operator removes the wrap, on the bare steel.

Instrument practice matters in this environment. We calibrate on a step block of the same material before each leg or riser, verify against a known thickness after, and use a couplant suited to wet, windy and sometimes hot surfaces. Heavy marine scale and rust scale are removed to bright metal at each reading point, because a transducer on loose scale reads the scale. On curved members, the contact surface is small, so a small-diameter transducer or a flat spot dressed on the pipe gives stable readings. Wall loss reported against the nominal thickness shows the owner where the steel is thinnest.

Weld examination on platform and module steel

Shear-wave UT of structural welds follows a written procedure that references ASME Section V Article 4 and the acceptance rules of AWS D1.1 where the structural specification invokes it. Tubular connections, where braces meet a chord at an angle, are the demanding case. The geometry changes the sound path around the joint, so the scan plan is developed with the Level III and demonstrated before use. Plate girders, deck framing, padeyes and stiffeners are more straightforward but still require attention to laminations in the base metal near the weld.

Fabrication yards on the Gulf Coast build new modules, deck sections and skid frames, and repair welds on retrieved equipment. UT is used for weld quality control there, and at the same sites for lamination checks of plate before welding. The ultrasonic weld inspection page describes the job in more detail.

Repair welds on retrieved or damaged members get the same treatment as new work with one extra step. The excavated area is checked for remaining thickness before welding, so the repair weld is made on steel that is thick enough, and the finished repair is examined after the required cooling period for delayed cracking. The report records the dates of weld completion and examination, which lets the owner and any reviewer see that the hold time was respected. Thick sections and higher-strength steels are where that discipline matters most.

Damage mechanisms the thickness data has to separate

Offshore wall loss has several distinct causes, and the grid is laid out to tell them apart. External atmospheric corrosion shows as broad, relatively uniform thinning on exposed pipe and deck steel. Corrosion under insulation and under fireproofing produces patches hidden until the cover comes off, usually where water tracks along supports and penetrations. Inside produced-water, flowline and gas-dehydration systems, carbon dioxide corrosion and microbial attack cut localized grooves and pits, often at the six o'clock position of horizontal lines and at welds, where flow and chemistry concentrate.

These patterns call for different readings. A uniform external loss is well described by a coarse grid. A groove along the bottom of a pipe needs a tighter circumferential spacing at that clock position. Pitting inside a vessel from the outside is sampled with a dense grid at low points and nozzle junctions, and the report states the grid spacing used so the next survey compares like with like.

Risers, conductors and caissons

Risers connect the seabed pipeline to the topsides, so they cross the splash zone and carry the full external corrosion load there. Conductors and caissons sit in the same environment. The inspection window is the exposed length from the cellar deck down to the waterline, plus accessible clamps and supports, where crevice corrosion hides behind riser guards. We survey the exposed run on a circumferential grid at fixed elevations, mark the minimum thickness on the member, and record clamp and support positions so the operator can compare the thinning against the sections it can see at the next survey.

Helidecks and accommodation steel

Helidecks are structural frames with an aluminum or steel deck. For the steel framing, UT measures section thickness at the bracing and the weld zones where salt spray collects and coatings fail first. The aluminum deck, which is nonmagnetic, is examined by penetrant testing for cracks at welds and fittings. Accommodation modules and living quarters are not a corrosion hot spot, but their support steel and lifting lugs are examined during transport and installation to the same procedures as the rest of the structure.

What a UT offshore report contains

  • Platform or yard, structure or line ID, elevation or clock position, and drawing reference
  • Procedure number and revision, and the code or integrity program governing acceptance
  • Instrument, transducer, calibration block, couplant and calibration check results
  • Technician name and SNT-TC-1A level, with the Level III who approved the procedure
  • Thickness grids and scan sketches with the minimum reading highlighted
  • Weld indications with location, length, amplitude and accept or reject against the named criteria

What to send for an offshore UT quote

  • Platform location or yard address, and whether the scope is offshore or onshore
  • Structure drawings, riser and piping lists or CML locations, and weld maps
  • Material, nominal thickness, coating and insulation, and operating temperature
  • Code and acceptance criteria, and the operator's inspection plan reference
  • Access method: scaffold, work basket, personnel transfer, and who provides rigging
  • Safety training, permits and transport requirements for offshore personnel

Offshore logistics and safety planning

Getting to a platform is a project of its own. The operator controls transport by helicopter or crew boat, personnel-on-board limits, bed space and baggage allowances, and the safety training it requires of visitors, which can include offshore survival or helicopter egress training where the operator demands it. Atlantis arranges these requirements with the operator, and we state what we have and do not have at the quote stage; we do not assume them. Weather cancels flights and boats, so a campaign needs float days. At onshore yards the issues are the usual ones: permits, scaffold, hot work, and heat or rain on exposed decks.

Where we work in the US for offshore

  • Houston: operator offices and the large Gulf fabrication supply chain that feed platform projects.
  • New Orleans: the center of Gulf shelf operations in Louisiana, with supply bases and service companies along the coast.
  • Mobile: Alabama yards and shipbuilders, and the gateway to eastern Gulf fabrication.
  • Lake Charles: Calcasieu fabrication and heavy-lift sites close to Louisiana offshore routes.
  • Corpus Christi: south Texas yards and ports that serve Gulf platforms and wind and energy modules.
  • Pascagoula: Mississippi's shipbuilding and marine fabrication base on the Gulf.

Training your own UT technicians

Operators and fabricators who want their own technicians can begin with UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with practice on the ultrasonic testing simulator. The employer certifies its personnel under SNT-TC-1A, and our oil and gas NDT training page describes the training path. For weld programs, see the national ultrasonic testing services page and the Article 5 thickness measurement guide.

What we do not do

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, does not run in-line inspection tools, and does not offer underwater or specialist techniques outside UT, MT and PT. We do not decide whether a damaged leg is fit to stay in service. That belongs to the operator's engineer, who uses our data.

faq.q: Does Atlantis perform UT on Gulf of Mexico platforms?
faq.a: Yes, on topsides and above-water structure, as long as the operator arranges access, transport and permits. Technicians are mobilized for the agreed scope and work to the operator's inspection program and BSEE requirements.

faq.q: Can you measure thickness in the splash zone?
faq.a: Above the waterline and where the structure is exposed, yes, after marine growth and rust scale are removed to bright metal. Underwater sections require diver or remote-vehicle work, which we do not offer.

faq.q: What codes govern offshore UT in the US?
faq.a: BSEE 30 CFR Part 250 regulates Gulf of Mexico operations, API RP 2A and the API structural integrity practice guide platforms, AWS D1.1 covers structural welds, and ASME B31.3 covers piping. ASME Section V sets the UT method.

faq.q: Can UT find cracks in tubular joints?
faq.a: Shear-wave UT can examine tubular welds, but joint geometry changes the sound path, so the scan plan is developed with a Level III and demonstrated first. Some critical joints also get magnetic particle testing of the weld toe.

faq.q: Who decides whether thinning is acceptable?
faq.a: The operator's engineer or integrity group decides, using our readings. Atlantis reports minimum thickness and location against nominal and does not set remaining life, intervals or fitness for service.

faq.q: What safety training does offshore work need?
faq.a: It is set by the operator, and can include offshore survival or helicopter egress training. We confirm the requirement at the quote stage and arrange it with the operator rather than assuming we already hold it.

faq.q: Do you inspect at fabrication yards as well as offshore?
faq.a: Yes. Weld quality control on new modules, deck sections and repairs is common at Gulf Coast yards and supply bases, and the same procedures and reports apply onshore.

faq.q: What do you need for an offshore UT quote?
faq.a: The platform or yard location, drawings or piping lists, materials and thicknesses, coating and insulation, code and acceptance criteria, access method and the operator's transport and safety requirements.

faq.q: When should we choose UT instead of MT or PT offshore?
faq.a: Use UT when you need wall thickness or internal weld flaws, and MT or PT when you need surface cracks. Many structural programs combine UT with MT on carbon steel and PT on aluminum or stainless.
